summary: Defines an IMAP extension letting a client use the result of the last SEARCH as input to a later command, without the server sending the message list back to the client first. This saves round trips and lets commands be pipelined. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Rather than reading a list aloud and having the librarian write it down again, you say, now do that to the books we just found.

questions: what does the imap dollar sign mean
how to reuse imap search results
subtitle: A small IMAP extension that lets a client say "use the messages my last search found" with a single dollar sign.

tldr.problem: Clients often search a mailbox and then fetch, copy or delete the found messages. With plain IMAP the server sends the list to the client, which must parse it, reformat it and send it back, and cannot pipeline the two commands.
tldr.mechanism: A new SAVE result option tells the server to remember the search result in a search result variable, and the marker $ stands for that saved list in later commands.
tldr.outcome: This saves bandwidth and round trips, allows pipelining, and lets servers optimize. The server must keep extra state, which is a possible denial of service concern. The RFC updates RFC 3501.

today: RFC 5182 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2008. It updates RFC 3501, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Many IMAP clients use the result of a SEARCH as input to another operation, such as fetching, deleting or copying the found messages. Plain RFC 3501 can do this, but badly. The server sends the list of found messages, the client parses and reformats it, and then sends it back. The client also cannot pipeline the search with the next command, so the server may miss optimizations.

RFC 5182 adds a SAVE result option. It tells the server to remember the result of a SEARCH or UID SEARCH (and commands based on search, such as SORT and THREAD) in an internal search result variable. The client can then write $ wherever a message sequence or UID sequence is allowed, and the server substitutes the saved list.

The listed advantages are: no wasted bandwidth and delay, pipelining of a search with a later FETCH, STORE, COPY, SEARCH or UID EXPUNGE, no need for the client to reformat results, and room for the server to decide which pipelined commands may run out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of copying a long list from one note to another, you write "the same ones as before" and the helper knows what you mean.

sections.title: The Search Result Variable
sections.content:
A server announces the extension by returning SEARCHRES in its CAPABILITY response. Such a server MUST also implement the ESEARCH extension (RFC 4731).

The rules for the variable are:

  • It is reset to the empty sequence after a successful SELECT or EXAMINE.
  • A successful SEARCH with SAVE sets it to the messages found, which may be none.
  • A SEARCH that gets a BAD response, a SEARCH without SAVE that gets NO, or a successful SEARCH without SAVE, MUST NOT change it.
  • A SEARCH with SAVE that gets NO sets it to the empty sequence.
  • Expunged messages are removed from it automatically. A server that stores message numbers MUST adjust them as in RFC 3501, Section 7.4.1.
  • A new UIDVALIDITY value sent while the mailbox is open resets it to the empty list.

An empty $ is a valid but non-matching list, so FETCH $ just returns a tagged OK with no FETCH responses. Also, $ can mean message sequence numbers or UIDs depending on where it is used. A SEARCH (SAVE) result can feed a UID FETCH, and a UID SEARCH (SAVE) result can feed a FETCH. With no other result option, SAVE also suppresses the normal SEARCH response.
sections.plainLanguage: The server keeps one sticky note with the last list of found messages. A new successful save replaces it, expunged messages get crossed off, and opening a mailbox gives you a blank note.

sections.title: Using the Dollar Sign
sections.content:
The basic pattern is to search with RETURN (SAVE) and then fetch with $. Because the second command depends on the first, the server MUST execute them in the order received, as RFC 3501 Section 5.5 requires. The client MAY pipeline them as long as no ambiguity arises.

$ can also feed another search (UID SEARCH $ SMALLER 4096) or be combined with other numbers using OR inside a search. A pipelined sequence like SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) KEYWORD $Junk, COPY $ "Junk" and STORE $ +FLAGS.Silent (\Deleted) moves and flags the matching messages without any list crossing the wire. If two SAVE searches are pipelined, the second one overrides the first. Two searches with no dependency between them may run in any order.

A failed saved search empties the variable. In the RFC's example, a search with an unsupported CHARSET gets a NO and leaves $ empty. The suggested workarounds are to give the CHARSET in the first SEARCH RETURN (SAVE) of a related sequence, or better, to always use CHARSET UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask for all the red marbles, then say "put those in the jar." If your first question gets muddled, the second one gets nothing, so ask clearly the first time.

sections.title: Working With ESEARCH
sections.content:
The SAVE option does not change which MIN, MAX, ALL or COUNT items the server returns. It does decide what $ holds, though.

With SAVE MIN alone, $ holds the single minimum message. With SAVE MAX alone, it holds the maximum. With both MIN and MAX and no other option, it holds those one or two messages. If ALL or COUNT is also given, $ always holds every message found. The RFC notes that this last rule may affect ESEARCH servers that optimize how COUNT is computed.

A search that returns ALL but has no SAVE leaves $ unchanged. A server MAY refuse to save a result, for example when it hits an internal limit on saved results. It then MUST return a tagged NO with the NOTSAVED response code and set the variable to the empty sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only ask for the first or last item, the sticky note holds just those. If you ask for everything or a count, the note holds the whole list.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The syntax is given in ABNF and is small. It adds the capability SEARCHRES, extends sequence-set with the marker seq-last-command (which is just "$"), defines SAVE as a search-return-opt as in RFC 4466, and adds the response code NOTSAVED. Strings are case-insensitive, and implementations MUST accept them that way.
sections.plainLanguage: The formal rules just add one new word, one new option and one new symbol to the language IMAP already speaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension makes the server keep extra state, and that may make Denial of Service attacks simpler. To limit the damage, a server MAY cap the number of saved searches across all connections at any given time. When the cap is exceeded it returns a tagged NO with NOTSAVED to a SEARCH RETURN (SAVE).

The RFC believes the extension raises no other security concerns beyond those already discussed in RFC 3501. For IANA, it defines the SEARCHRES capability and has it added to the IMAP4 Capabilities Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a sticky note for everyone costs the server memory, so it is allowed to say "no more notes" if too many pile up.
